title: Converse, Inverse and Contrapositive
short: p → q is equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p, but not to its converse q → p or its inverse ¬p → ¬q.
trouble: Treating the converse as equivalent is affirming the consequent in disguise. A truth table shows the row where they differ.

blocks.html: Every conditional has three relatives, made by swapping and negating its parts. Only one of them says the same thing as the original. This builds on Logical Equivalence.
A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive $ eg q o eg p$, but not to its converse $q o p$ or its inverse $ eg p o eg q$. (The converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other.)

$p 	o q$ is false in exactly one row: $p$ true, $q$ false. The contrapositive $
eg q 	o 
eg p$ is false when $
eg q$ is true and $
eg p$ is false, which is the same row. So they have the same column. The converse $q 	o p$ is false in a different row, $q$ true and $p$ false, so it makes a different claim. "If it is a dog, it is a mammal" is true; its converse "if it is a mammal, it is a dog" is not.

blocks.name: lg-truthtable
blocks.cap: The original and the contrapositive match; the converse differs in two rows.

blocks.title: All three relatives
blocks.q: Write the converse, inverse and contrapositive of $r \to \neg s$.
steps:
Inverse (negate both): $
eg r 	o 
eg 
eg s$, which may be written $
eg r 	o s$.

Contrapositive (swap and negate): $
eg 
eg s 	o 
eg r$, that is $s 	o 
eg r$.
blocks.a: The contrapositive $s \to \neg r$ is the only one equivalent to the original.

blocks.title: In English
blocks.q: "If you have a ticket, you get into the show." What is the contrapositive?
steps: Swap the parts and negate both.
blocks.a: "If you do not get into the show, you do not have a ticket."

blocks.html: Treating the converse as equivalent. That is affirming the consequent in disguise: from "if it rained, the street is wet" you cannot get "if the street is wet, it rained", since a sprinkler could have wet it. The truth table shows the row ($q$ T, $p$ F) where the two disagree.

blocks.title: A converse that fails
blocks.q: "If a shape is a square, it has four sides." Is the converse true?
steps: The converse is "If a shape has four sides, it is a square."
A rectangle that is not a square has four sides.
blocks.a: No. The original is true and its converse is false, so they cannot be equivalent.

blocks.html: There is a neat pattern in the table: the inverse is the contrapositive of the converse. Swap $q \to p$ and negate both parts and you get $\neg p \to \neg q$. That is why the converse and the inverse always agree with each other, while the original and the contrapositive agree with each other.

The contrapositive is useful in proofs. When $p \to q$ is hard to show directly, showing $\neg q \to \neg p$ proves the same thing. Later this becomes a rule of replacement, Transposition (Transposition and Material Implication (Trans, Impl)).
